sections.process: Of 14,999 original records, 5,000 lacked targets and one had a malformed target; 9,998 were eligible. Customer ID was assigned the identifier role and default the label. A stratified split with seed 2202 reserved 1,999 customers for testing. Five-fold stratified cross-validation used only the 7,999 training records. Imputation and nominal-vocabulary removal were fitted within training folds; logistic regression additionally used dummy encoding and standardisation. The fitted preprocessing models transformed validation records unchanged. Fourteen financial and demographic predictors were retained. No resampling or holdout-driven tuning occurred (Kohavi, 1995).
sections.recommendations:
Banks should treat these models as exploratory evidence. All four fixed test evaluations missed every default, so the present operating rules cannot support automatic lending decisions. Accuracy near 89% largely reflects the prevalence of non-default customers. Precision and recall deserve priority when defaults are uncommon (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015).

Collect payment histories, debt-service ratios, loan duration, interest rates and the dates at which each predictor became available. Audit missingness and confirm that features precede default. A subsequent study should predefine loss-sensitive thresholds and precision-recall criteria on new training data, then validate once on an untouched later cohort. The current test set must not become a tuning resource.

Investigate age, income, borrowing purpose and financial buffers as associations requiring confirmation. Coefficients do not establish that changing these characteristics changes default risk. Evaluate calibration and expected loss, including the costs of missed defaults and incorrectly rejecting reliable applicants. Human reviewers should assess affordability using verified evidence while any predictive system remains outside operational eligibility decisions.
sections.ethics:
A model that misses every default can create false confidence and expose customers to unaffordable credit. The present classifiers should therefore remain research tools. A future system would need documented performance criteria, independent validation and clear accountability before it influenced lending.

Age and education can encode demographic differences, while income and financial circumstances can reflect historical disadvantage. Removing a sensitive attribute alone does not remove proxy discrimination (Mehrabi et al., 2019). Compare error rates, calibration and outcomes across legally and ethically appropriate groups, with sufficient sample sizes and uncertainty estimates. The supplied data do not establish that any model satisfies a fairness criterion.

Use only necessary customer information, restrict access, document retention and record consent or other appropriate authority for processing. Explanations should distinguish predictive associations from causal reasons and should allow customers to challenge inaccurate records. A small model coefficient does not justify a categorical claim about a person.

Keep a human review and appeal process, log model versions and decisions, and monitor changes in customer populations. Review disagreements between predicted risk and verified affordability. Transparent disclosure of the failed default recall is essential: a high overall accuracy should not be presented as proof of safe or equitable lending.
sections.predictors: The native logistic model assigned negative weights to standardised age (-0.214), academic associate education (-0.235) and masters education (-0.181). These conditional associations depend on coding and correlated inputs; they do not demonstrate causal protection. The selected decision tree contained only a non-default leaf, so it identified no decisive split predictor (Quinlan, 1986). This contrast limits business interpretation: the logistic model ranks some customers differently, while the tree provides no segmentation. RapidMiner implements this operator through myKLR, so the exported weights should not be described as estimates from a separately fitted conventional regression (RapidMiner, n.d.).
sections.comparison: Training-only cross-validation gave logistic regression AUC 0.647 and pooled default F1 1.40%; the decision tree achieved AUC 0.500 and no default detections. I therefore selected logistic regression for investigation before examining the test set. On 1,999 held-out customers, logistic regression achieved 89.34% accuracy and AUC 0.625, versus 89.39% and 0.500 for the tree. Both had zero default recall. Logistic regression produced one false positive; the tree predicted non-default throughout. Native F1 was undefined because no defaults were correctly identified; count-derived F1 was zero. Logistic regression offers some ranking information, but neither model is suitable for bank lending. Majority-class accuracy obscures failed minority detection, so precision-recall evidence is essential (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015). The holdout was not used to alter model settings or selection (Kohavi, 1995).
